Compromised jscrambler 8.14.0 npm Release Drops Rust Infostealer During Install

The Hacker News
2026-07-11 15 use cases 5 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

The jscrambler npm package was compromised, and simply installing its&nbsp;8.14.0&nbsp;release runs an infostealer on your machine. Published on July 11, 2026, the malicious version carries a&nbsp;preinstall&nbsp;hook that drops and executes a native binary, one build each for Windows, macOS, and Linux. jscrambler compromised npm version (8.14.0/8.16-8.20) install/resolve on build host AIDelivery High
Hunts package-manager processes acquiring the trojanized jscrambler releases (8.14.0 and the SafeDep-corroborated 8.16.0/8.17.0/8.18.0/8.20.0) by version-pinned command line. Article-specific because it keys on the exact CLI package and malicious version strings still live on npm, so any lockfile/CI job pinned to them keeps pulling the stealer. Rationale: Keys on the exact malicious package@version strings from the article plus the SafeDep-corroborated sibling versions; because 8.14.0 was never unpublished, any pinned install still pulls it, making the version string a high-fidelity anchor. Cross-checked against: • https://safedep.io/jscrambler-npm-supply-chain-compromise/ • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/jscrambler-npm-package-publishes-malicious-preinstall-binary
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1195.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security team intentionally pulling 8.14.0 into an isolated sandbox for malware analysis
  • Dependency-scanning/SCA tooling that references the version string in its own command line while auditing (not installing)
  • A developer running `npm view jscrambler@8.14.0` to inspect metadata without installing
  • Internal mirror/proxy warm-up jobs enumerating all published versions
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("npm view","npm info","audit","snyk","osv-scanner"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the host actually resolved/installed vs. merely referenced the version — check for node_modules/jscrambler/dist/setup.js and a Node child process spawning a temp binary in the minutes after. 2) Contain: isolate the host/CI runner; kill any process running out of the temp directory; remove jscrambler@8.14.0 (and 8.16-8.20) from lockfiles and caches and repin to 8.15.0 or 8.13.0. 3) Hunt: pivot to UC 'Outbound C2' for connections to 37.27.122.124/57.128.246.79, and treat all secrets reachable by the build/CI identity as stolen — rotate cloud, npm, GitHub, and AI-tool/MCP keys.

| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "jscrambler"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("jscrambler@8.14.0","jscrambler@8.16.0","jscrambler@8.17.0","jscrambler@8.18.0","jscrambler@8.20.0")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where CommandLine has "jscrambler"

| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName

Rust infostealer binary executed from jscrambler npm preinstall (setup.js) hook AIExploitation High
Detects the payload running by exact SHA-256 of the three native builds, or by a Node/npm process invoking dist/setup.js that spawns an unsigned binary from a temp directory. Article-specific: setup.js is the named loader and the hashes are the published Windows/macOS/Linux stealer builds. Rationale: Uses the three published payload SHA-256s (exact IOCs) plus the article's named loader chain node/npm -> setup.js -> unsigned temp binary; both are article-specific and rarely occur benignly on build hosts. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/jscrambler-npm-package-publishes-malicious-preinstall-binary • https://safedep.io/jscrambler-npm-supply-chain-compromise/
ATT&CKT1204.003 T1546.016 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate native postinstall builds (e.g. esbuild, node-gyp, sharp) writing helper binaries to temp during install — filter by hash-only for high confidence
  • In-repo test fixtures deliberately containing the sample hashes for detection validation
  • EDR sandbox detonation of the sample generating the hash match
  • Node tools that legitimately shell out to a temp-extracted CLI from a setup script
Suppression filter
| where not (FolderPath has_any ("node-gyp","esbuild","prebuilds") and SHA256 !in ("b7ca95d1b23c8e67416a25cedf741de0917c2096bbc9d24649eea7853d054903","c8fd47d36bdf7c825378593ab82ed8c24d1dc52e26b507812393e24e1d5201fd","fbbcf4d8f98168f78f5c0c47a9ae56d59ec8ac84a7c9ca6b797fedfb8d62d2bd"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: if the SHA-256 branch fired, this is a confirmed payload — capture the temp file path/PID before it self-cleans. If only the behavioral branch fired, verify the parent is genuinely jscrambler's setup.js and the child is unsigned. 2) Contain: isolate host, kill the temp process tree, block the two C2 IPs at egress, and quarantine the temp binary. 3) Hunt: check Task Scheduler for a hidden every-minute task and ~/Library/LaunchAgents for new plists (see persistence UC); enumerate what secrets the process touched.

    or (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","npm.exe") and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "setup.js" and FolderPath has_any ("Temp","/tmp/","/var/folders/"))

Trojanized jscrambler package artifacts (setup.js/intro.js) written to node_modules AIDelivery Medium
Detects the two added files in the compromised package by exact SHA-256, or by their creation under node_modules/jscrambler/dist. intro.js is a ~7.8MB gzip container of native binaries, not JavaScript — its presence is the tampering fingerprint. Rationale: setup.js and intro.js SHA-256s are exact published IOCs; the node_modules/jscrambler/dist path plus the deceptively-named intro.js (a gzip binary container, not JS) is the specific tampering signature StepSecurity and SafeDep confirmed absent from upstream. Cross-checked against: • https://safedep.io/jscrambler-npm-supply-chain-compromise/ • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/jscrambler-npm-package-publishes-malicious-preinstall-binary
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1036 T1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A clean jscrambler release that legitimately ships a dist/setup.js in future versions (hash branch avoids this)
  • Local test/CI fixtures seeded with the sample files for validation
  • Backup/restore tooling rehydrating an old infected node_modules snapshot (still a true positive worth reviewing)
  • Security researchers extracting the package for analysis
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm which jscrambler version resolved on the host and whether dist/setup.js already executed (correlate with a Node child spawning a temp binary). 2) Contain: delete the infected node_modules/jscrambler, purge npm cache, repin to 8.15.0/8.13.0, and rebuild in a clean runner. 3) Hunt: sweep all developer/CI hosts and shared artifact caches for the two hashes; if found anywhere, assume install ran and rotate reachable secrets.

Outbound C2 to jscrambler stealer IPs or Tor bootstrap from build host AICommand & Control Medium
Detects the dropped stealer beaconing to the two hard-coded attacker IPs, or reaching Tor bootstrap infrastructure (check/archive.torproject.org). These are the first published network indicators for the campaign and are unusual egress for a CI/build host. Rationale: Uses the two hard-coded C2 IPs (37.27.122.124, 57.128.246.79) confirmed by both StepSecurity and SafeDep, plus the Tor bootstrap domains; direct-IP egress and Tor bootstrap from a build/CI host is high-fidelity. CloudWatch omitted: this is endpoint/network egress telemetry, not CloudTrail. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/jscrambler-npm-package-publishes-malicious-preinstall-binary • https://safedep.io/jscrambler-npm-supply-chain-compromise/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1573.002 T1090.003
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate use of Tor Browser or a Tor-enabled tool by a developer (check.torproject.org is the standard connectivity check)
  • Threat-intel/sandbox appliances deliberately connecting to the C2 IPs for enrichment
  • Shared NAT egress IP where the two /32s coincidentally match a proxy (verify exact /32)
  • A pentest/red-team exercise reusing the same IOCs
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("tor.exe","firefox.exe","browser.exe") and RemoteUrl in~ ("check.torproject.org","archive.torproject.org"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process — if it runs from a temp directory or was spawned by node/npm, treat as confirmed. 2) Contain: block 37.27.122.124 and 57.128.246.79 at egress, isolate the host, and kill the temp process. 3) Hunt: pull all hosts that contacted either IP in the last 30d; for each, rotate every secret the build identity could reach (cloud, npm, GitHub, Bitwarden, AI/MCP keys) and check for the persistence artifacts.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP in ("37.27.122.124","57.128.246.79")
    or RemoteUrl in~ ("check.torproject.org","archive.torproject.org")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DstIpAddr in ("37.27.122.124","57.128.246.79")
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkApplicationProtocol, DvcAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Temp-directory binary reading across multiple developer secret stores AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts a single process running from a temp directory that touches two or more distinct secret-store classes — AI coding-tool/MCP configs (Claude, Cursor, Windsurf, VS Code, Zed), browser credential stores, cloud CLI configs, and wallets/Bitwarden/SSH. Article-specific because the stealer's target list explicitly spans these and the AI-tool config theft is novel. Rationale: Encodes the article's explicit target list (AWS/Azure/GCP configs, MetaMask/Phantom/Exodus, Bitwarden, browsers, and the novel Claude/Cursor/Windsurf/VS Code/Zed MCP configs) and requires a single temp-run process to hit >=2 distinct classes, which no legitimate build step does. Sigma/Datadog omitted: cross-category aggregation isn't single-event-shape and Datadog Sysmon EID11 captures writes not reads. Cross-checked against: • https://safedep.io/jscrambler-npm-supply-chain-compromise/ • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/jscrambler-npm-package-publishes-malicious-preinstall-binary
ATT&CKT1005 T1555.003 T1552.001 T1528 T1539
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate credential-sync or backup agent that happens to run from a temp path enumerating multiple stores
  • Endpoint DLP/AV scanning that reads across browser and config directories
  • A developer's own dotfile/secrets management tool launched from a temp-extracted installer
  • IDE first-run indexing touching browser and cloud config folders
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("msmpeng.exe","mssense.exe","code.exe","onedrive.exe") and InitiatingProcessSHA256 !in (dynamic([]))
Response runbook
1) Triage: check whether the initiating temp binary was spawned by node/npm during a jscrambler install and whether it subsequently connected to the C2 IPs. 2) Contain: isolate host, kill the process, and immediately begin secret rotation for every store it read (cloud keys, AI-tool/MCP tokens, Bitwarden, browser sessions, SSH). 3) Hunt: search the same InitiatingProcessSHA256 org-wide; review cloud audit logs (AWS/Azure/GCP) for use of the stolen keys post-incident.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any ("Temp","/tmp/","/var/folders/")
| extend SecretStore = case(
    FolderPath has_any ("Claude","Cursor","Windsurf","Zed",".cursor",".claude","codeium"), "ai_tool_config",
    FolderPath has_any ("Chrome","BraveSoftware","Edge","Mozilla"), "browser_secrets",
    FolderPath has_any (".aws","gcloud",".azure"), "cloud_creds",
    FolderPath has_any ("Bitwarden","MetaMask","Exodus","Phantom",".ssh"), "wallet_or_vault",
    "other")
| where SecretStore != "other"
| summarize StoreTypes = dcount(SecretStore), Stores = make_set(SecretStore), SampleFiles = make_set(FolderPath, 10) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessSHA256
| where StoreTypes >= 2
| order by StoreTypes desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("Temp","/tmp/","/var/folders/")
| extend SecretStore = case(
    TargetFilePath has_any ("Claude","Cursor","Windsurf","Zed",".cursor",".claude","codeium"), "ai_tool_config",
    TargetFilePath has_any ("Chrome","BraveSoftware","Edge","Mozilla"), "browser_secrets",
    TargetFilePath has_any (".aws","gcloud",".azure"), "cloud_creds",
    TargetFilePath has_any ("Bitwarden","MetaMask","Exodus","Phantom",".ssh"), "wallet_or_vault",
    "other")
| where SecretStore != "other"
| summarize StoreTypes = dcount(SecretStore), Stores = make_set(SecretStore) by DvcHostname, ActingProcessName
| where StoreTypes >= 2
| order by StoreTypes desc
#event_simpleName=FileOpenInfo
| ContextImageFileName=/[\\/](Temp|tmp|var[\\/]folders)[\\/]/i
| TargetFileName=/(Claude|Cursor|Windsurf|Zed|\.cursor|\.claude|codeium|Chrome|BraveSoftware|Edge|Mozilla|\.aws|gcloud|\.azure|Bitwarden|MetaMask|Exodus|Phantom|\.ssh)/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName], function=count(field=TargetFileName, distinct=true))

| tstats summariesonly=true count from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.process_path="*Temp*" OR Filesystem.process_path="*/tmp/*" OR Filesystem.process_path="*/var/folders/*") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.process_path Filesystem.file_path | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | eval store=case(match(file_path,"(?i)(Claude|Cursor|Windsurf|Zed|Code.User|\.cursor|\.claude|codeium)"),"ai_tool_config", match(file_path,"(?i)(Chrome|BraveSoftware|Edge|Mozilla)"),"browser_secrets", match(file_path,"(?i)(\.aws|gcloud|\.azure)"),"cloud_creds", match(file_path,"(?i)(Bitwarden|MetaMask|Exodus|Phantom|\.ssh)"),"wallet_or_vault", 1=1,"other") | where store!="other" | stats dc(store) as storeTypes values(store) as stores values(file_path) as files by dest process_path | where storeTypes>=2

Cloud instance-metadata (IMDS) access by temp-directory binary AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects a process running from a temp directory reaching the cloud metadata endpoint (169.254.169.254 / metadata.google.internal). The article calls out that the stealer specifically targets the metadata endpoints CI runners use to lift federated cloud credentials. Rationale: The article explicitly states the stealer targets 'the metadata endpoints CI runners use'; pairing the well-known link-local IMDS IP with a temp-directory initiating process is the article-specific pivot. Sentinel omitted: ImNetworkSession carries no initiating-process field, so the temp-binary constraint (which removes the flood of legitimate SDK IMDS calls) cannot be expressed on available Sentinel network telemetry. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/jscrambler-npm-package-publishes-malicious-preinstall-binary
ATT&CKT1552.005 T1552.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate cloud SDK/CLI tools transiently extracted to temp that query IMDS on CI runners
  • Instance bootstrap/agent installers run from temp during provisioning
  • Monitoring agents (CloudWatch agent, ops agents) hitting IMDS from an unusual path
  • Container runtimes proxying IMDS for workloads
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("aws.exe","az.exe","gcloud.exe","amazon-ssm-agent.exe","amazon-cloudwatch-agent.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the initiating temp binary is not a known cloud SDK; check whether it also touched local cloud config files or beaconed to the C2 IPs. 2) Contain: isolate the runner, revoke the instance/role credentials exposed via IMDS, and rotate any derived cloud keys. 3) Hunt: review cloud audit logs (CloudTrail/Azure Activity/GCP audit) for API calls from the runner's role after the IMDS hit; enforce IMDSv2 / hop-limit on affected instances.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "169.254.169.254" or RemoteUrl in~ ("metadata.google.internal")
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any ("Temp","/tmp/","/var/folders/")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl
| order by Timestamp desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "169.254.169.254" or RemoteUrl in~ ("metadata.google.internal")
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any ("Temp","/tmp/","/var/folders/")
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Cloud IMDS Access by Temp-Directory Binary
id: 4a91c7e2-6b3d-4f88-8a1c-5d2e9b7f0a31
description: Detects a process executing from a temp directory contacting the cloud instance-metadata endpoint, matching the jscrambler stealer credential sweep.

logsource:

detection:

level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:3 @DestinationIp:169.254.169.254 @Image:(*\\Temp\\* OR *\\temp\\* OR *\\TEMP\\*)
#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4
| RemoteAddressIP4=/^169\.254\.169\.254$/
| ContextImageFileName=/[\\/](Temp|tmp|var[\\/]folders)[\\/]/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, RemoteAddressIP4], function=count())
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where All_Traffic.dest_ip="169.254.169.254" AND (All_Traffic.process="*Temp*" OR All_Traffic.process="*/tmp/*" OR All_Traffic.process="*/var/folders/*") by All_Traffic.src_ip All_Traffic.dest_ip All_Traffic.process | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where All_Traffic.dest_ip="169.254.169.254" AND (All_Traffic.process="*Temp*" OR All_Traffic.process="*/tmp/*" OR All_Traffic.process="*/var/folders/*") by All_Traffic.src_ip All_Traffic.dest_ip All_Traffic.process | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Persistence artifact (scheduled task / LaunchAgent) written by a temp-directory binary AIInstallation High
Detects the stealer's persistence step: a process running from a temp directory creating a Windows scheduled-task file (System32\Tasks) or a macOS LaunchAgent plist (~/Library/LaunchAgents). The article describes a hidden every-minute Windows task and a login-reload macOS LaunchAgent. Rationale: Pairs the two persistence mechanisms named in the article (Windows scheduled task under System32\Tasks, macOS LaunchAgent plist) with a temp-directory initiating process — the loader drops the payload to temp before it installs persistence, so a temp binary writing a task/plist is high-fidelity and rare on build hosts. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/jscrambler-npm-package-publishes-malicious-preinstall-binary • https://safedep.io/jscrambler-npm-supply-chain-compromise/
ATT&CKT1053.005 T1543.001 T1564.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate installer extracted to temp that registers a scheduled task during setup (e.g. updater bootstrappers)
  • macOS app first-run from a temp-mounted DMG writing a LaunchAgent
  • Software-deployment tooling staging task XML from a temp working directory
  • Backup/EDR agents self-installing persistence from a temp installer
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("msiexec.exe","setup.exe","tiworker.exe","trustedinstaller.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: open the created task/plist and inspect its target — if it points at a randomly-named hidden temp binary or runs every minute, treat as confirmed. 2) Contain: delete the task/LaunchAgent, kill and quarantine the temp binary, and isolate the host. 3) Hunt: search for the every-minute schedule and hidden .{random}/.exe temp files org-wide; correlate with the C2 IPs and jscrambler install events, then rotate exposed secrets.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where (FolderPath has_all ("System32","Tasks")) or (FolderPath has "LaunchAgents")
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any ("Temp","/tmp/","/var/folders/")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, ActionType, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where (TargetFilePath has "System32" and TargetFilePath has "Tasks") or (TargetFilePath has "LaunchAgents")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("Temp","/tmp/","/var/folders/")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, DvcAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Persistence Artifact Written by Temp-Directory Binary
id: 7e0d3c92-1a54-4b6f-9c88-2f4a1e6b0d55
description: Detects a temp-directory process creating a Windows scheduled-task file, matching the jscrambler stealer persistence.
references:

logsource:

detection:

level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 @TargetFilename:(*System32*Tasks* OR *Library*LaunchAgents*) @Image:(*Temp* OR *temp* OR *TEMP*)
#event_simpleName=FileWritten
| TargetFileName=/([\\/]System32[\\/]Tasks[\\/]|[\\/]Library[\\/]LaunchAgents[\\/])/i
| ContextImageFileName=/[\\/](Temp|tmp|var[\\/]folders)[\\/]/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, TargetFileName, ContextImageFileName], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where ((Filesystem.file_path="*System32*Tasks*") OR (Filesystem.file_path="*/Library/LaunchAgents/*")) AND (Filesystem.process_path="*Temp*" OR Filesystem.process_path="*/tmp/*" OR Filesystem.process_path="*/var/folders/*") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.process_path Filesystem.file_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where ((Filesystem.file_path="*System32*Tasks*") OR (Filesystem.file_path="*/Library/LaunchAgents/*")) AND (Filesystem.process_path="*Temp*" OR Filesystem.process_path="*/tmp/*" OR Filesystem.process_path="*/var/folders/*") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.process_path Filesystem.file_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("a742de963f14a92d24ebcbc7b44ac867e23a20d31d1b0094a13a4f83287f4e60", "a41a523ef9517aab37ed6eea0ec881821bdcb7aefcb5c5f603adc7907f868c86", "fbbcf4d8f98168f78f5c0c47a9ae56d59ec8ac84a7c9ca6b797fedfb8d62d2bd", "b7ca95d1b23c8e67416a25cedf741de0917c2096bbc9d24649eea7853d054903", "c8fd47d36bdf7c825378593ab82ed8c24d1dc52e26b507812393e24e1d5201fd") or SHA1 in~ ("a742de963f14a92d24ebcbc7b44ac867e23a20d31d1b0094a13a4f83287f4e60", "a41a523ef9517aab37ed6eea0ec881821bdcb7aefcb5c5f603adc7907f868c86", "fbbcf4d8f98168f78f5c0c47a9ae56d59ec8ac84a7c9ca6b797fedfb8d62d2bd", "b7ca95d1b23c8e67416a25cedf741de0917c2096bbc9d24649eea7853d054903", "c8fd47d36bdf7c825378593ab82ed8c24d1dc52e26b507812393e24e1d5201fd") or MD5 in~ ("a742de963f14a92d24ebcbc7b44ac867e23a20d31d1b0094a13a4f83287f4e60", "a41a523ef9517aab37ed6eea0ec881821bdcb7aefcb5c5f603adc7907f868c86", "fbbcf4d8f98168f78f5c0c47a9ae56d59ec8ac84a7c9ca6b797fedfb8d62d2bd", "b7ca95d1b23c8e67416a25cedf741de0917c2096bbc9d24649eea7853d054903", "c8fd47d36bdf7c825378593ab82ed8c24d1dc52e26b507812393e24e1d5201fd")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("a742de963f14a92d24ebcbc7b44ac867e23a20d31d1b0094a13a4f83287f4e60", "a41a523ef9517aab37ed6eea0ec881821bdcb7aefcb5c5f603adc7907f868c86", "fbbcf4d8f98168f78f5c0c47a9ae56d59ec8ac84a7c9ca6b797fedfb8d62d2bd", "b7ca95d1b23c8e67416a25cedf741de0917c2096bbc9d24649eea7853d054903", "c8fd47d36bdf7c825378593ab82ed8c24d1dc52e26b507812393e24e1d5201fd") or SHA1 in~ ("a742de963f14a92d24ebcbc7b44ac867e23a20d31d1b0094a13a4f83287f4e60", "a41a523ef9517aab37ed6eea0ec881821bdcb7aefcb5c5f603adc7907f868c86", "fbbcf4d8f98168f78f5c0c47a9ae56d59ec8ac84a7c9ca6b797fedfb8d62d2bd", "b7ca95d1b23c8e67416a25cedf741de0917c2096bbc9d24649eea7853d054903", "c8fd47d36bdf7c825378593ab82ed8c24d1dc52e26b507812393e24e1d5201fd") or MD5 in~ ("a742de963f14a92d24ebcbc7b44ac867e23a20d31d1b0094a13a4f83287f4e60", "a41a523ef9517aab37ed6eea0ec881821bdcb7aefcb5c5f603adc7907f868c86", "fbbcf4d8f98168f78f5c0c47a9ae56d59ec8ac84a7c9ca6b797fedfb8d62d2bd", "b7ca95d1b23c8e67416a25cedf741de0917c2096bbc9d24649eea7853d054903", "c8fd47d36bdf7c825378593ab82ed8c24d1dc52e26b507812393e24e1d5201fd")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["a742de963f14a92d24ebcbc7b44ac867e23a20d31d1b0094a13a4f83287f4e60", "a41a523ef9517aab37ed6eea0ec881821bdcb7aefcb5c5f603adc7907f868c86", "fbbcf4d8f98168f78f5c0c47a9ae56d59ec8ac84a7c9ca6b797fedfb8d62d2bd", "b7ca95d1b23c8e67416a25cedf741de0917c2096bbc9d24649eea7853d054903", "c8fd47d36bdf7c825378593ab82ed8c24d1dc52e26b507812393e24e1d5201fd"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

cms_plugin.exe Rust stager execution + payload pull from 193.42.25.65 AIInstallation High
Hunts the custom 'cms_plugin.exe' implant that masqueraded as a Complaint Management System portal update on Balochistan Police infrastructure. The Rust stager variant downloads a next stage from 193.42.25.65 and prints 'Update Complete! Please refresh the page'. Fires on the named binary executing or any host reaching the stager download IP. Rationale: cms_plugin.exe is a unique implant filename and 193.42.25.65 is the confirmed Rust-stager download server named in the SentinelLABS report; both are non-generic, so a match is effectively a true positive. Cross-checked SentinelOne report and The Record write-up. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sentinelone.com/labs/one-target-china-india-espionage-converge-on-pakistani-law-enforcement/ • https://therecord.media/china-india-ran-separate-spy-campaigns-against-same-police-force
ATT&CKT1105 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimately-named plugin binary in an unrelated product also called cms_plugin.exe (rare; validate hash and path)
  • Security researcher / IR analyst detonating the sample in a sandbox VM enrolled in EDR
  • Threat-intel enrichment appliance actively probing 193.42.25.65 for research
  • Proxy/NAT egress IP collision where 193.42.25.65 is re-used by a benign CDN in future (validate at trigger time)
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith "C:\\Sandbox\\" and DeviceName !in~ ("IR-SANDBOX-01")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the process tree, SHA256, and folder path for cms_plugin.exe; confirm parent (likely w3wp.exe/web-app service on a CMS/web server) and whether the host is an internet-facing police web application server. 2) Contain: isolate the host, block 193.42.25.65 at the perimeter, and preserve the binary for reversing. 3) Hunt: sweep all web servers for cms_plugin.exe uploads, search web logs on cms.balochistanpolice.gov.pk-style portals for the file, and pivot on the SHA1s and the full campaign C2 IP set (see C2 UC).
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "193.42.25.65" or InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "cms_plugin.exe"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessSHA256, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl
| order by Timestamp desc
union
(SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where tolower(NewProcessName) endswith "\\cms_plugin.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, Signal="process", NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName, Dest=""),
(CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DestinationIP == "193.42.25.65"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer=SourceHostName, Account=SourceUserName, Signal="network", NewProcessName=ProcessName, CommandLine="", ParentProcessName="", Dest=DestinationIP)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Fake 360Safe.exe (.NET) reflectively loading AsyncRAT AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the second cms_plugin.exe variant: a .NET executable that masquerades as '360Safe.exe' (a legitimate Qihoo 360 Total Security binary) to reflectively load an in-memory AsyncRAT client. Detects a process named 360Safe.exe whose file metadata is NOT Qihoo/360 or which runs from outside the legitimate 360 install path. Rationale: The report states one implant variant masquerades specifically as 360Safe.exe (Qihoo 360) to reflectively load AsyncRAT; a 360Safe.exe binary running outside the genuine Qihoo install path (or lacking Qihoo file metadata) is a high-fidelity masquerade signal, especially in a Pakistani gov environment unlikely to run Chinese AV. Corroborated by SentinelOne report and Kaspersky's Mysterious Elephant AsyncRAT/Remcos tradecraft. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sentinelone.com/labs/one-target-china-india-espionage-converge-on-pakistani-law-enforcement/ • https://securelist.com/mysterious-elephant-apt-ttps-and-tools/117596/
ATT&CKT1036.005 T1620
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Genuine Qihoo 360 Total Security installed to a non-default drive/path (validate publisher signature)
  • Portable/standalone 360 Total Security run from a USB or Downloads folder by a user
  • Software-deployment tool staging the real 360Safe.exe in a temp cache before install
  • AV bake-off / procurement testing of 360 Total Security by IT
Suppression filter
| where not(ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName has_any ("360","Qihoo"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: check the digital signature and ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName of the 360Safe.exe image — genuine is signed by Qihoo/360; the implant will be unsigned or mis-signed. Inspect for .NET/CLR module loads and outbound connections. 2) Contain: isolate the host, capture memory (AsyncRAT is in-memory), block associated C2 IPs. 3) Hunt: search DeviceImageLoadEvents for clr.dll/mscoree loading into 360Safe.exe, and correlate with cms_plugin.exe drops and the campaign C2 IP set.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "360Safe.exe"
| where not(ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName has_any ("360","Qihoo")) or FolderPath !startswith "C:\\Program Files"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName, ProcessVersionInfoProductName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where tolower(NewProcessName) endswith "\\360safe.exe"
| where not(tolower(NewProcessName) startswith "c:\\program files (x86)\\360\\") and not(tolower(NewProcessName) startswith "c:\\program files\\360\\")
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
title: Masquerading 360Safe.exe Outside Qihoo 360 Install Path

Beaconing to Balochistan Police espionage C2 / stager IP set AICommand & Control High
Hunts outbound connections to the confirmed command-and-control and staging IPs across the four converging clusters (Cobalt Strike C2 142.171.183.8, Rust-stager host 193.42.25.65, plus the campaign infrastructure block) targeting Pakistani law enforcement. Any internal host reaching these IPs warrants investigation. Rationale: 142.171.183.8 is the named Cobalt Strike C2 and 193.42.25.65 the stager host; the remaining IPs are the pre-extracted campaign infrastructure. These are static, second-source-consistent IOCs, so egress to any of them is high-fidelity for this specific converging-actor campaign. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sentinelone.com/labs/one-target-china-india-espionage-converge-on-pakistani-law-enforcement/ • https://therecord.media/china-india-ran-separate-spy-campaigns-against-same-police-force
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1105
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • An IOC IP later reassigned to a shared hosting/CDN provider serving benign sites (re-validate WHOIS at trigger time)
  • Internal threat-intel platform or vulnerability scanner actively probing the C2 IPs
  • Security researcher pivoting on the infrastructure from a corporate egress IP
  • Firewall/proxy that logs a blocked (denied) attempt — confirm DeviceAction/outcome is allow before escalating
Suppression filter
DeviceNetworkEvents | where ActionType in ("ConnectionSuccess","ConnectionAttempt") and RemoteIPType == "Public"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the source host and the InitiatingProcess making the connection; check whether the connection succeeded vs was blocked, and beacon regularity (jitter/interval). 2) Contain: block all listed IPs at the perimeter, isolate any host with a successful/repeated connection, and snapshot memory for the process (PlugX/ShadowPad/Cobalt Strike/AsyncRAT are memory-resident). 3) Hunt: pivot on the initiating process hash against the campaign SHA1 list, sweep for cms_plugin.exe and fake 360Safe.exe, and review the FortiMail email gateway and web-app servers for the initial foothold.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP in ("142.171.183.8","193.42.25.65","41.216.188.140","89.31.121.220","45.125.32.218","172.111.233.36","172.111.233.96","172.111.233.12","172.111.233.105","172.111.233.26","172.94.9.49","172.94.9.43","172.94.9.19","45.74.6.17")
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), Conns=count(), Ports=make_set(RemotePort,10) by DeviceName, RemoteIP, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by LastSeen desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DestinationIP in ("142.171.183.8","193.42.25.65","41.216.188.140","89.31.121.220","45.125.32.218","172.111.233.36","172.111.233.96","172.111.233.12","172.111.233.105","172.111.233.26","172.94.9.49","172.94.9.43","172.94.9.19","45.74.6.17")
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), Conns=count(), Ports=make_set(DestinationPort,10) by SourceIP, SourceHostName, DestinationIP, DeviceProduct
| order by LastSeen desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

Outbound traffic to attacker infrastructure named in the article.

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
let BadIPs     = dynamic(["142.171.183.8", "193.42.25.65", "41.216.188.140", "89.31.121.220", "45.125.32.218", "172.111.233.36", "172.111.233.96", "172.111.233.12", "172.111.233.105", "172.111.233.26", "172.94.9.49", "172.94.9.43", "172.94.9.19", "45.74.6.17"]);

let BadHashes = dynamic(["23f6781919a50b118d8d4e6a7e9ae63b71ecc885", "4039454c9189e64285e93fc075a30b93f814b5b5", "58cb2d95063b9df807b7aa8dc106b74ce988a491", "000fad96a85dd6933c22d3dbec9aed47b7f1f066", "08570471f39bb6725f07b8cddbea99ed48c22686", "23f4766c011d193f076dfc735dc460e2a41ead79", "47f8cb0c2dcf62702f58cfc1603d6325755f6820", "5d60ff36ff519c2e13e7f66cfa0bb46be79592a7", "63b88d00331de88af696dfb7a896935d830e485f", "8c329db96e093fa25268e078405a33c518dbb5c9", "d66ab0cd2e44dc8389c111b7ea34c7bcb0b35311", "2bab40c55637398f0497cff9c8cbea564d595c7f", "539bd79fbb684edea94eb37518134b97e94b9dd8", "6fe2e74d009abbd56de01fd7404a1245e9b47c79", "71757adba833b46f961e840d0f055bcce0b529c4", "c6c197e61079a0a33108c2c87b5e3c7056a138ec"]);
union

        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Critical

jscrambler npm package publishes malicious preinstall binary

StepSecurity
2026-07-11 13 use cases 5 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

On July 11, 2026, version 8.14.0 of jscrambler was published to npm carrying a malicious preinstall hook that drops and executes a platform-specific native binary on Linux, Windows, and macOS. jscrambler is the official CLI client for the Jscrambler Code Integrity API, a commercial JavaScript obfuscation and web-app protection service, with a clean version history dating back to 0.1.0. The compromised release was flagged by StepSecurity's AI Release Analyzer with a suspicion score of 0 (the maximum suspicion rating) on publish.

Malicious jscrambler@8.14.0 native-binary container 'intro.js' dropped into node_modules AIDelivery High
Hunts the supply-chain artifact: a 7.8 MB file named intro.js written under the jscrambler package's dist directory. In a JS-obfuscation CLI this file has no legitimate purpose and is a Rust native-binary container masquerading behind a .js extension (magic bytes 1B 43 53 49 01). This is the on-disk fingerprint of the compromised release before the payload runs. Rationale: Anchors on the article's exact artifact — file named intro.js under the jscrambler package dir at anomalous multi-MB size — a masqueraded native container, not JS. Cross-checked with thehackernews.com and safedep.io. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/compromised-jscrambler-8140-npm-release.html • https://safedep.io/jscrambler-npm-supply-chain-compromise/
ATT&CKT1195.001 T1036.008
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A different, legitimately large intro.js bundle in an unrelated package that happens to sit under a folder path containing 'jscrambler' (rare)
  • Security researcher intentionally staging the 8.14.0 sample in a sandbox path
  • Backup/restore tooling re-writing an already-quarantined copy of the file
  • A local monorepo package coincidentally named jscrambler with a large generated intro.js
Suppression filter
| where not (FolderPath has @"\quarantine\" or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("MsMpEng.exe","MsSense.exe"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the file is the 8.14.0 container — check magic bytes 1B 43 53 49 01 and hash the extracted payload against the three known SHA256s; grep package-lock.json for jscrambler 8.14.0. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill any detached temp-dir process, and remove node_modules + npm cache; block the two C2 IPs and Tor endpoints. 3) Hunt: pivot on DeviceProcessEvents for a temp-dir dotfile spawned by node.exe and on any outbound to 37.27.122.124 / 57.128.246.79; treat the host as compromised and rotate all browser-stored and CI/CD credentials.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "intro.js"
| where FolderPath has @"\jscrambler\"
| where FileSize > 1048576   // 1MB — a real intro.js in a JS CLI is a few KB; the malicious container is 7.8MB
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, FileName, FileSize, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName =~ "intro.js"
| where TargetFilePath has @"\jscrambler\"
| where TargetFileSize > 1048576   // 7.8MB container vs KB-sized legit JS
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSize, TargetFileSHA256, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

npm/node preinstall spawns detached hidden binary from OS temp directory AIInstallation High
Hunts the execution stage: the preinstall loader decompresses a platform binary to a randomly-named dotfile in the OS temp dir (with .exe on Windows) and launches it detached from the npm tree. Detects node.exe spawning a child whose path is a leading-dot random-named executable under Temp — the exact behaviour the loader (dist/setup.js) exhibits. Rationale: Combines the article's precise loader behaviour — parent node.exe, OS temp dir, leading-dot random [a-z0-9]{6,} name, .exe suffix on Windows, detached — into one high-fidelity execution predicate that no benign npm lifecycle script matches. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/compromised-jscrambler-8140-npm-release.html • https://safedep.io/jscrambler-npm-supply-chain-compromise/
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1564.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate npm package with a native postinstall that stages a helper binary in temp (rare, usually named not dotfile+random)
  • node-based test harness writing throwaway executables to temp during CI
  • Electron builders that unpack signed helper exes to temp
  • Developer running a local tool that shells out to a temp-compiled binary
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("electron-builder","node-gyp","prebuild-install"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the dotfile from temp and hash it against the three known payload SHA256s; confirm parent chain traces to an npm install of jscrambler 8.14.0. 2) Contain: kill the detached process, isolate the host, and remove the temp binary + node_modules; block the C2 IPs/Tor endpoints at the egress. 3) Hunt: search DeviceNetworkEvents from that binary to 37.27.122.124 / 57.128.246.79, check Task Scheduler / LaunchAgents for persistence, and rotate every browser-stored and pipeline credential on the host.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","npm.exe")
| where FolderPath has @"\Temp\"
| where FileName matches regex @"^\.[a-z0-9]{6,}\.exe$"   // random dotfile written by the loader
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\\node.exe","\\npm.exe")
| where NewProcessName has @"\Temp\"
| where NewProcessName matches regex @"\\\.[a-z0-9]{6,}\.exe$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Execution or write of known jscrambler Rust stealer payload by SHA256 AIInstallation Medium
Deterministic hash-based catch for the three extracted platform payloads (ELF, PE32+, Mach-O arm64) from dist/intro.js. Fires on process creation or file write matching any known-bad hash regardless of drop path or name — the highest-confidence backstop for hosts that ran 8.14.0. Rationale: Uses the three verbatim payload SHA256 IOCs from the article's IOC table across process and file telemetry — zero ambiguity, deterministic true positives on any host that dropped or ran the stealer. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/compromised-jscrambler-8140-npm-release.html • https://safedep.io/jscrambler-npm-supply-chain-compromise/
ATT&CKT1204.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Malware analyst detonating the sample in an EDR-monitored sandbox
  • Threat-intel platform re-hashing a stored copy during enrichment
  • Backup agent reading the quarantined payload copy (file-read event only)
  • Purple-team validation exercise deliberately staging the IOC
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the match is a live host, not a sandbox/analysis VM; identify the drop path and parent process. 2) Contain: isolate the host, terminate the process, quarantine the file, and block the C2 IPs/Tor endpoints. 3) Hunt: enumerate all hosts that installed jscrambler 8.14.0 via software inventory / lockfiles, check for Task Scheduler + LaunchAgent persistence, and force rotation of browser credentials, crypto wallets, npm/GitHub and cloud tokens.

Outbound C2 to jscrambler stealer IPs / Tor endpoints during or after npm install AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts the command-and-control stage: connections to the two hardcoded stealer IPs (37.27.122.124, 57.128.246.79) and the Tor reachability domains (check/archive.torproject.org) observed via Harden-Runner. Strongest on the raw IPs, which have no benign use in a build pipeline. Rationale: Uses the article's verbatim C2 IOCs confirmed by StepSecurity Harden-Runner and echoed by thehackernews.com. The two raw IPs are the high-fidelity signal; the torproject domains add coverage but can be noisy on developer machines running Tor Browser. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/compromised-jscrambler-8140-npm-release.html • https://safedep.io/jscrambler-npm-supply-chain-compromise/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1090.003
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer legitimately running Tor Browser reaching check.torproject.org / archive.torproject.org (domain clause only — the two IPs have no benign use)
  • Security scanner or threat-intel connectivity test probing the blocklisted IPs
  • Researcher detonating the sample in a monitored lab
  • Corporate proxy pre-fetching the torproject domains for categorization
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("tor.exe","firefox.exe","tor-browser.exe") and RemoteIP !in ("37.27.122.124","57.128.246.79"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process — a temp-dir dotfile or node.exe confirms the stealer; a browser hitting only the torproject domains is likely benign. 2) Contain: block 37.27.122.124 and 57.128.246.79 at the firewall/egress, isolate the host, and kill the process. 3) Hunt: correlate back to a jscrambler 8.14.0 install and the temp-dir binary, pull any exfil volume from flow logs, and rotate all credentials the stealer could reach (browsers, wallets, CI/CD, cloud, npm/GitHub tokens).
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP in ("37.27.122.124","57.128.246.79")
    or RemoteUrl in~ ("check.torproject.org","archive.torproject.org")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl
| order by Timestamp desc
union
  (ImNetworkSession | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where DstIpAddr in ("37.27.122.124","57.128.246.79") | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkApplicationProtocol, Indicator=DstIpAddr),
  (ImDnsActivity | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where DnsQuery in~ ("check.torproject.org","archive.torproject.org") | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr=DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber=int(53), NetworkApplicationProtocol="dns", Indicator=DnsQuery)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

| where RemoteIP in ("37.27.122.124", "57.128.246.79") or RemoteUrl has_any ("")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
let BadIPs     = dynamic(["37.27.122.124", "57.128.246.79"]);
let BadDomains = dynamic([""]);
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DstIpAddr in (BadIPs)
   or Url has_any (BadDomains)
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, Url, NetworkProtocol
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")

| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"

PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command Exploitation High
Encoded or obfuscated PowerShell — common across loaders, recon, and post-exploitation.
ATT&CKT1059.001 T1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(-enc|encodedcommand|frombase64string|-nop|-w\s+hidden|invoke-expression|iex\s*\(|downloadstring|net\.webclient)"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\pwsh.exe"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(-enc|encodedcommand|frombase64string|-nop|-w\s+hidden|invoke-expression|iex\s*\(|downloadstring|net\.webclient)"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName,
          CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Obfuscated / Encoded PowerShell Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d08
status: experimental
description: |
    PowerShell launched with -EncodedCommand, base64 strings, hidden
    window, no-profile, bypass policy, IEX / Invoke-Expression / Net
    .WebClient.DownloadString — combinations indicating evasion.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1027
    - attack.execution
    - attack.defense-evasion
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_image:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
    selection_args:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - '-enc '
            - 'EncodedCommand'
            - 'FromBase64String'
            - 'Invoke-Expression'
            - 'IEX('
            - 'DownloadString'
            - 'Net.WebClient'
            - '-w hidden'
            - '-WindowStyle Hidden'
            - '-nop'
            - '-NoProfile'
            - '-ep bypass'
            - '-ExecutionPolicy Bypass'
    condition: selection_image and selection_args
falsepositives:
    - DevOps tooling that legitimately uses encoded command for
      cross-shell escaping
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*-enc *" OR Processes.process="*EncodedCommand*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*Net.WebClient*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*-enc *" OR Processes.process="*EncodedCommand*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*Net.WebClient*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium
Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
// Replace `"setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe"` with the vendor binaries observed in the
// article (matching shape with the Defender query).
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\bitsadmin.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Trusted Vendor Binary Launching Unusual Children
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d09
status: experimental
description: |
    A signed vendor binary (in the article's named-vendors list)
    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when
    paired with a recent CVE / supply-chain advisory naming the same
    vendor.
references:

            - '\mshta.exe'

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("fbbcf4d8f98168f78f5c0c47a9ae56d59ec8ac84a7c9ca6b797fedfb8d62d2bd", "b7ca95d1b23c8e67416a25cedf741de0917c2096bbc9d24649eea7853d054903", "c8fd47d36bdf7c825378593ab82ed8c24d1dc52e26b507812393e24e1d5201fd") or SHA1 in~ ("fbbcf4d8f98168f78f5c0c47a9ae56d59ec8ac84a7c9ca6b797fedfb8d62d2bd", "b7ca95d1b23c8e67416a25cedf741de0917c2096bbc9d24649eea7853d054903", "c8fd47d36bdf7c825378593ab82ed8c24d1dc52e26b507812393e24e1d5201fd") or MD5 in~ ("fbbcf4d8f98168f78f5c0c47a9ae56d59ec8ac84a7c9ca6b797fedfb8d62d2bd", "b7ca95d1b23c8e67416a25cedf741de0917c2096bbc9d24649eea7853d054903", "c8fd47d36bdf7c825378593ab82ed8c24d1dc52e26b507812393e24e1d5201fd")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("fbbcf4d8f98168f78f5c0c47a9ae56d59ec8ac84a7c9ca6b797fedfb8d62d2bd", "b7ca95d1b23c8e67416a25cedf741de0917c2096bbc9d24649eea7853d054903", "c8fd47d36bdf7c825378593ab82ed8c24d1dc52e26b507812393e24e1d5201fd") or SHA1 in~ ("fbbcf4d8f98168f78f5c0c47a9ae56d59ec8ac84a7c9ca6b797fedfb8d62d2bd", "b7ca95d1b23c8e67416a25cedf741de0917c2096bbc9d24649eea7853d054903", "c8fd47d36bdf7c825378593ab82ed8c24d1dc52e26b507812393e24e1d5201fd") or MD5 in~ ("fbbcf4d8f98168f78f5c0c47a9ae56d59ec8ac84a7c9ca6b797fedfb8d62d2bd", "b7ca95d1b23c8e67416a25cedf741de0917c2096bbc9d24649eea7853d054903", "c8fd47d36bdf7c825378593ab82ed8c24d1dc52e26b507812393e24e1d5201fd")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["fbbcf4d8f98168f78f5c0c47a9ae56d59ec8ac84a7c9ca6b797fedfb8d62d2bd", "b7ca95d1b23c8e67416a25cedf741de0917c2096bbc9d24649eea7853d054903", "c8fd47d36bdf7c825378593ab82ed8c24d1dc52e26b507812393e24e1d5201fd"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Critical Zimbra Flaw Could Let Crafted Emails Run Malicious Code in User Sessions

The Hacker News
2026-07-11 10 use cases 3 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Zimbra is urging customers to apply updates to address a critical security vulnerability impacting the Classic Web Client that could result in arbitrary code execution. The vulnerability has been described as a case of stored cross-site scripting (XSS) that could allow specially crafted emails to execute malicious scripts in a user's session. It has yet to be assigned a CVE identifier. "The
