Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → [LLM] Unpatched Zimbra Collaboration below 10.1.19 exposed to Classic Web Client XSS · Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] XSS payload strings in HTTP requests to Zimbra Classic Web Client endpoints
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code.
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → Suspicious browser extension installation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Cross-origin external script fetch referred from Zimbra webmail session · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
XSS payload strings in HTTP requests to Zimbra Classic Web Client endpoints AIDelivery Medium
Hunts crafted-email stored-XSS delivery against the Zimbra Classic Web Client by matching script/event-handler injection tokens in requests to Zimbra web endpoints (/h/, /service/soap, /public/). Article-specific: the flaw only affects the Classic Web Client and is triggered when a crafted email is rendered, mirroring the confirmed CVE-2023-37580 exploitation shape. Rationale: Uses the article's specific attack surface (Zimbra Classic Web Client endpoints /h/ and /service/soap) plus the confirmed historical exploitation payload shape (<script src=, onerror=) from Google TAG's CVE-2023-37580 write-up; endpoint+payload pairing is high-fidelity vs a bare token match. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/zimbra-urges-customers-to-patch-critical-web-client-xss-flaw/ • https://blog.google/threat-analysis-group/zimbra-0-day-used-to-target-international-government-organizations/ • https://gbhackers.com/zimbra-releases-security-patch-stored-xss/
ATT&CKT1189 T1059.007
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • WAF/IDS appliances logging blocked XSS probes against the Zimbra front-end
  • Authorized vulnerability scanners (Nessus/Qualys/Burp) fuzzing Zimbra with script tokens
  • Legitimate emails whose subject/body quotes JavaScript and is reflected in a search URL
  • Pen-test engagements against the mail estate
  • Marketing/newsletter emails containing on* HTML attributes rendered via the web client
Suppression filter
| where RequestClientApplication !has_any ("Nessus","Qualys","Burp","nikto","sqlmap","Nuclei") | where DeviceAction !in~ ("blocked","denied","deny","drop")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full RequestURL and SourceIP; decode the parameter and confirm whether a real <script>/event-handler payload was reflected or stored vs a scanner probe. Identify the target mailbox/user and whether the request returned 200. 2) Contain: if a stored payload is confirmed, block the SourceIP at the WAF, quarantine/purge the offending message from the target mailbox, and confirm ZCS is on 10.1.19. 3) Hunt: search the same SourceIP and payload host for other recipients, and pivot to proxy logs for outbound requests to any external host referenced inside the payload (see cross-origin script-fetch UC).
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where (DeviceVendor has "zimbra" or DestinationServiceName has "zimbra" or DestinationHostName has "zimbra" or RequestURL has_any ("/h/","/service/soap","/service/preauth","/public/","/zimbra/"))
| where RequestURL has_any ("<script","%3Cscript","onerror=","onload=","onmouseover=","javascript:","<svg","<img ","document.cookie")
   or Message has_any ("<script","onerror=","document.cookie")
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, DestinationHostName, DestinationServiceName, RequestMethod, RequestURL, RequestClientApplication, DeviceAction, Message
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: XSS Payload in HTTP Request to Zimbra Classic Web Client
id: 5f2c9a71-3e8b-4c0d-9a2e-7b1f4d6c8a10
status: experimental
description: Detects script/event-handler injection tokens in requests to Zimbra Classic Web Client endpoints, consistent with the crafted-email stored XSS fixed in ZCS 10.1.19 and the earlier exploited CVE-2023-37580.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/critical-zimbra-flaw-could-let-crafted_0483473395.html
  - https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/zimbra-urges-customers-to-patch-critical-web-client-xss-flaw/
  - https://blog.google/threat-analysis-group/zimbra-0-day-used-to-target-international-government-organizations/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/12
tags:
  - attack.t1189
  - attack.t1059.007
  - attack.initial_access
logsource:
  category: proxy
detection:
  selection_endpoint:
    cs-uri-stem|contains:
      - '/h/'
      - '/service/soap'
      - '/service/preauth'
      - '/public/'
      - '/zimbra/'
  selection_payload:
    cs-uri-query|contains:
      - '<script'
      - '%3Cscript'
      - 'onerror='
      - 'onload='
      - 'onmouseover='
      - 'javascript:'
      - 'document.cookie'
  condition: selection_endpoint and selection_payload
falsepositives:
  - WAF/IDS logging of blocked probe traffic
  - Security scanners (Nessus, Burp) testing the Zimbra host
  - Emails discussing scripting quoted back in a URL parameter
level: high
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web.Web where (Web.url IN ("*/h/*","*/service/soap*","*/service/preauth*","*/public/*","*/zimbra/*") OR Web.site="*zimbra*") AND (Web.url IN ("*<script*","*%3Cscript*","*onerror=*","*onload=*","*onmouseover=*","*javascript:*","*document.cookie*") OR Web.uri_query IN ("*<script*","*%3Cscript*","*onerror=*","*javascript:*")) by Web.src, Web.dest, Web.site, Web.url, Web.http_method, Web.http_user_agent | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web.Web where (Web.url IN ("*/h/*","*/service/soap*","*/service/preauth*","*/public/*","*/zimbra/*") OR Web.site="*zimbra*") AND (Web.url IN ("*<script*","*%3Cscript*","*onerror=*","*onload=*","*onmouseover=*","*javascript:*","*document.cookie*") OR Web.uri_query IN ("*<script*","*%3Cscript*","*onerror=*","*javascript:*")) by Web.src, Web.dest, Web.site, Web.url, Web.http_method, Web.http_user_agent | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | sort - count
Cross-origin external script fetch referred from Zimbra webmail session AICommand & Control Medium
Detects a browser loading a script/resource from an external host where the HTTP Referer is the Zimbra Classic Web Client — the exact behaviour of the stored-XSS payload that injects <script src="attacker/...js">. Article-specific: exploitation runs 'in the user's session' and the confirmed 2023 Zimbra campaign pulled a remote .js from an attacker domain. Rationale: Grounded in the confirmed exploitation IOC pattern ("/><script src="https://obsorth.opwtjnpoc.ml/...js">) from Google TAG's Zimbra XSS report: a cross-origin .js load whose Referer is the Zimbra web client is a direct signature of XSS payload retrieval in-session. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.google/threat-analysis-group/zimbra-0-day-used-to-target-international-government-organizations/ • https://thehackernews.com/2023/11/zero-day-flaw-in-zimbra-email-software.html • https://socprime.com/blog/cve-2023-37580-detection-four-hackering-groups-exploit-a-zimbra-zero-day-vulnerability-targeting-state-bodies/
ATT&CKT1539 T1059.007
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate CDN-hosted assets/analytics loaded by a customized Zimbra theme or zimlet
  • Corporate DLP/monitoring beacons injected into pages
  • Third-party integration zimlets that pull JS from a vendor domain
  • Ad/tracking scripts on external content rendered in-message
  • Browser extensions rewriting Referer and fetching helper scripts
Suppression filter
| where DstHost !endswith "zimbra.com" | where DstHost !endswith "gstatic.com" and DstHost !endswith "googleapis.com"
Response runbook
1) Triage: resolve DstHost — check domain age/reputation and whether any other org host has ever fetched it; inspect the .js content if retrievable. Identify the SrcIp/user and confirm they were in an active Zimbra session. 2) Contain: block DstHost at proxy/DNS, invalidate the user's Zimbra session/auth tokens and force re-auth, and purge the triggering message. 3) Hunt: enumerate every user whose Referer=Zimbra fetched the same DstHost; review Zimbra audit log for forwarding-rule/preference changes on those accounts (session-hijack follow-through).
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where HttpRequestHeaderReferer has_any ("/h/","/zimbra/","/service/","/mail")
| where Url matches regex @"(?i)\.js(\?|$)" or FileMimeType has "javascript"
| extend RefHost = tolower(tostring(parse_url(HttpRequestHeaderReferer)["Host"])), DstHost = tolower(coalesce(DstHostname, tostring(parse_url(Url)["Host"])))
| where isnotempty(DstHost) and isnotempty(RefHost) and DstHost != RefHost
| summarize Requests = count(), SampleUrl = any(Url), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated) by SrcIpAddr, RefHost, DstHost
| order by FirstSeen desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web.Web where (Web.http_referrer IN ("*/h/*","*/zimbra/*","*/service/*")) AND Web.url="*.js*" by Web.src, Web.http_referrer, Web.url, Web.dest, Web.site | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | eval ref_host=lower(replace(http_referrer,"^https?://([^/]+).*","\1")), dst_host=lower(replace(url,"^https?://([^/]+).*","\1")) | where ref_host!=dst_host | sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web.Web where (Web.http_referrer IN ("*/h/*","*/zimbra/*","*/service/*")) AND Web.url="*.js*" by Web.src, Web.http_referrer, Web.url, Web.dest, Web.site | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | eval ref_host=lower(replace(http_referrer,"^https?://([^/]+).*","\1")), dst_host=lower(replace(url,"^https?://([^/]+).*","\1")) | where ref_host!=dst_host | sort - count
Unpatched Zimbra Collaboration below 10.1.19 exposed to Classic Web Client XSS AIReconnaissance High
Exposure hunt that lists managed hosts running Zimbra Collaboration Suite below the fixed version 10.1.19, which remain vulnerable to the crafted-email stored XSS. Article-specific: Zimbra named 10.1.19 as the fixed build and the flaw only affects the Classic Web Client. Rationale: Directly uses the article's named fixed version (ZCS 10.1.19); a numeric major/minor/patch comparison flags any host below the patched build so the SOC can prioritise the Classic-Web-Client attack surface. Cross-checked against: • https://forums.zimbra.org/viewtopic.php?t=74629 • https://securityaffairs.com/195130/hacking/update-now-critical-zimbra-classic-web-client-flaw-could-expose-mailboxes.html
ATT&CKT1189
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Hosts running only the Modern Web Client (not exploitable) but still flagged on version
  • Inventory lag where a just-patched host still reports the old build
  • Non-production/lab Zimbra instances with no internet exposure
  • Version strings with non-standard suffixes that parse oddly (e.g. GA/patch tags)
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm each flagged host actually serves the Classic Web Client (zimbraFeatureClassicWebClient) and its internet exposure. 2) Contain: schedule upgrade to ZCS 10.1.19 (zimbra-patch + zimbra-mbox-webclient-war); as interim mitigation disable the Classic Web Client for users where feasible. 3) Hunt: for any host that stayed unpatched, run the XSS-payload and cross-origin-script-fetch detections against its proxy/audit logs for the exposure window.
DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where SoftwareVendor has "zimbra" or SoftwareName has "zimbra"
| extend Parts = split(SoftwareVersion, ".")
| extend Major = toint(Parts[0]), Minor = toint(Parts[1]), Patch = toint(extract(@"^(\d+)", 1, tostring(Parts[2])))
| where isnotnull(Major) and (Major < 10 or (Major == 10 and Minor < 1) or (Major == 10 and Minor == 1 and Patch < 19))
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, EndOfSupportStatus, EndOfSupportDate
| sort by SoftwareVersion asc
Suspicious browser extension installation Installation Medium
Side-loaded / unsigned extensions, often masquerading as wallets, productivity tools.
ATT&CKT1176
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry DeviceRegistryEvents
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where RegistryKey has_any ("\Software\Google\Chrome\Extensions\","\Software\Microsoft\Edge\Extensions\","\Software\Mozilla\Firefox\Extensions\")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName
ImRegistryEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where RegistryKey has_any (@"\Software\Google\Chrome\Extensions\",
                              @"\Software\Microsoft\Edge\Extensions\",
                              @"\Software\Mozilla\Firefox\Extensions\")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, RegistryKey,
          RegistryValue, RegistryValueData, ActingProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies

Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"

SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → [LLM] Internal recon via Advanced IP Scanner (The Gentlemen) · Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Article-specific behavioural hunt — No Manners Here: The Ruthless Rise of The Gentlemen Ransomware
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] The Gentlemen RaaS: scheduled task named 'gentlemen*' · [LLM] GentleKiller BYOVD: vulnerable ThrottleStop.sys (CVE-2025-7771) load/drop · [LLM] Forensic destruction: wevtutil clearing Security/System/Application logs · Scheduled task created with suspicious image / encoded args · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] SystemBC C2 beacon to The Gentlemen infrastructure IPs · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Ransomware impact prep: Volume Shadow Copy deletion (vssadmin/wmic) · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft)
The Gentlemen RaaS: scheduled task named 'gentlemen*' AIInstallation High
Hunts creation, execution or deletion of any Windows scheduled task whose name matches the string gentlemen*, a persistence/execution artifact Unit 42 explicitly attributes to The Gentlemen (Storm-2697) RaaS. This is a hard-coded naming convention rather than a generic schtasks pattern, making it very high fidelity. Rationale: Unit 42's Execution recommendation names the exact string 'gentlemen*' for scheduled tasks as a high-severity alert; corroborated via ESET/Securelist write-ups of the same actor. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/the-gentlemen-ransomware/ • https://securelist.com/the-gentlemen-raas/120447/
ATT&CKT1053.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate software product genuinely named with the token 'gentlemen' (extremely rare in enterprise)
  • Security team creating a deception/canary task named gentlemen to trip this rule
  • Threat-hunt or purple-team exercise deliberately staging the artifact
  • Backup/RMM tools that let users free-name tasks and an operator typed 'gentlemen'
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("msiexec.exe","trustedinstaller.exe") and InitiatingProcessFolderPath startswith "C:\\Windows\\")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full task XML (schtasks /query /tn <name> /xml) and the InitiatingProcess — legitimate tasks are created by installers/GPO, not by cmd/powershell/rundll32 in Temp. 2) Contain: isolate the host, disable and delete the task, and snapshot for forensics before deletion. 3) Hunt: sweep all endpoints for the same task name, then pivot to the creating account and look for GentleKiller driver loads, wevtutil log clears and vssadmin shadow deletion on the same host.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("schtasks.exe","at.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "gentlemen"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID in (4698, 4699, 4702)
| where EventData has "gentlemen"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, EventID, Activity, EventData
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: The Gentlemen Ransomware Scheduled Task Naming Convention
id: 6f2c1a94-3b7e-4d21-9a55-7c1e0b2d4f10
description: Detects creation or execution of a scheduled task whose name matches the string gentlemen*, a persistence artifact attributed to The Gentlemen (Storm-2697) RaaS.
references:
  - https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/the-gentlemen-ransomware/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/12
tags:
  - attack.execution
  - attack.persistence
  - attack.t1053.005
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\schtasks.exe'
      - '\at.exe'
    CommandLine|contains: 'gentlemen'
  condition: selection
level: high
source:windows.security @EventID:4688 (@Image:(*\schtasks.exe OR *\SCHTASKS.EXE) OR @Image:(*\at.exe OR *\AT.EXE)) @CommandLine:(*gentlemen* OR *Gentlemen* OR *GENTLEMEN*)

GentleKiller BYOVD: vulnerable ThrottleStop.sys (CVE-2025-7771) load/drop AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the drop or load of the ThrottleStop.sys signed vulnerable driver used by The Gentlemen's GentleKiller EDR-killer framework (CVE-2025-7771) to gain ring-0 and terminate 400+ security processes. Also matches the campaign's known GentleKiller SHA256 hashes. Rationale: Article names GentleKiller and CVE-2025-7771 (ThrottleStop.sys); ESET and TheHackerNews confirm the driver name and BYOVD technique, and NVD confirms the CVE. Hashes drawn from the campaign IOC set are included as a secondary anchor. Cross-checked against: • https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/eset-research/killing-me-gently-inside-gentlemens-edr-killer-framework/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/the-gentlemen-raas-uses-gentlekiller.html • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2025-7771
ATT&CKT1562.001 T1068
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Genuine ThrottleStop CPU-tuning utility installed by an enthusiast on an engineering laptop
  • Overclocking/thermal-management software bundling the same signed driver
  • Hardware-vendor diagnostic packages that legitimately load ThrottleStop.sys
  • Red-team BYOVD tooling exercise
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith "C:\\Program Files" and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith "C:\\Program Files (x86)"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the loading/creating process — legit ThrottleStop is launched by the user from Program Files; a drop into Temp/ProgramData by rundll32/powershell/an unsigned parent is malicious. Check for EDR agent-health gaps around the same timestamp. 2) Contain: isolate the host, block the driver hash via WDAC/ASR, and verify EDR sensor is still reporting. 3) Hunt: enumerate other GentleKiller driver variants (HexKiller/ThrottleBlood/HavocKiller), review which security processes were terminated, and check for the gentlemen* scheduled task and shadow-copy deletion.
union DeviceImageLoadEvents, DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "throttlestop.sys"
   or SHA256 in ("22b38dad7da097ea03aa28d0614164cd25fafeb1383dbc15047e34c8050f6f67","51b9f246d6da85631131fcd1fabf0a67937d4bdde33625a44f7ee6a3a7baebd2","025fc0976c548fb5a880c83ea3eb21a5f23c5d53c4e51e862bb893c11adf712a","3ab9575225e00a83a4ac2b534da5a710bdcf6eb72884944c437b5fbe5c5c9235")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4697
| where ServiceFileName has "throttlestop"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ServiceName, ServiceFileName, ServiceType, ServiceStartType
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Forensic destruction: wevtutil clearing Security/System/Application logs AIInstallation High
Hunts execution of wevtutil to clear Windows event logs, a defense-evasion step Unit 42 recommends alerting on for The Gentlemen; corroborating reporting shows the encryptor runs 'wevtutil cl System / Application / Security' to destroy forensic evidence pre-encryption. Rationale: Unit 42 explicitly recommends behavioral alerts for wevtutil clearing Security/System logs; Check Point's DFIR report shows the concrete 'wevtutil cl System/Application/Security' commands, giving exact cmdline anchors. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/the-gentlemen-ransomware/ • https://research.checkpoint.com/2026/dfir-report-the-gentlemen/
ATT&CKT1070.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sysadmin manually clearing a bloated event log during troubleshooting
  • Log-management/SIEM onboarding scripts that rotate or clear logs
  • Golden-image/build pipeline clearing logs before sysprep
  • Software installers that reset application logs
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","rundll32.exe") or IsInitiatingProcessRemoteSession == true
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the parent process and account — legit clears come from an interactive admin or imaging script; a clear spawned by cmd.exe from a ransomware staging path or immediately after an EDR kill is malicious. Check EID 1102 for the corresponding audit-log-cleared event. 2) Contain: isolate the host, preserve any remaining logs and memory. 3) Hunt: pivot on the account/host for GentleKiller driver loads, vssadmin shadow deletion, and SystemBC C2 to confirm the ransomware chain.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "wevtutil.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("cl ","clear-log","cl System","cl Security","cl Application")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "wevtutil.exe"
| where CommandLine has_any ("cl ","clear-log")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Internal recon via Advanced IP Scanner (The Gentlemen) AIReconnaissance Medium
Hunts execution of Advanced IP Scanner, the network-mapping tool Unit 42 states The Gentlemen frequently use for internal reconnaissance prior to lateral movement. Anchored on the binary name and product-version metadata rather than generic scanning behaviour. Rationale: Unit 42's Discovery recommendation names Advanced IP Scanner specifically as a Gentlemen tool; the binary name plus product-version metadata is a stable anchor. Tiered hunting because IT teams also use it legitimately. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/the-gentlemen-ransomware/ • https://www.trendmicro.com/en_us/research/25/i/unmasking-the-gentlemen-ransomware.html
ATT&CKT1046
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IT/helpdesk staff mapping a subnet for asset inventory
  • MSP/RMM onboarding scan of a client network
  • Network engineer troubleshooting connectivity
  • Penetration test or authorized vulnerability scan
Suppression filter
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Temp\", @"\Downloads\", @"\Public\", @"\ProgramData\") or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has @"\Temp\"
Response runbook
1) Triage: check whether the executing account is IT/network staff and the host is an admin workstation — malicious use runs from a compromised user context or a server, often from Temp/Downloads. 2) Contain: if unexpected, isolate and review what ranges were scanned. 3) Hunt: within the same host/account window look for SMB self-propagation, GentleKiller driver loads and staging of the encryptor.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "advanced_ip_scanner.exe" or ProcessVersionInfoProductName has "Advanced IP Scanner"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "advanced_ip_scanner.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Ransomware impact prep: Volume Shadow Copy deletion (vssadmin/wmic) AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts destruction of Volume Shadow Copies via vssadmin, wmic or PowerShell WMI, an anti-recovery step Unit 42 recommends alerting on for The Gentlemen. Targets the concrete 'delete shadows' / 'shadowcopy delete' invocations that precede encryption. Rationale: Unit 42's Impact recommendation explicitly calls for behavioral alerts on vssadmin/wmic shadow-copy deletion; the 'delete shadows'/'shadowcopy delete' strings are canonical and article-endorsed for this actor. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/the-gentlemen-ransomware/ • https://research.checkpoint.com/2026/dfir-report-the-gentlemen/
ATT&CKT1490
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Veeam/commvault backup pre-snapshot cleanup of stale shadow copies
  • Sysadmin troubleshooting VSS storage exhaustion
  • Windows disk-cleanup or in-place upgrade removing old restore points
  • Custom maintenance script pruning shadow storage
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !has_any ("veeam","vsnapvss","cvd.exe","acronis","backup")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify parent process and account — backup software (veeam*, vsnapvss) legitimately manages VSS; deletion by cmd.exe/an encryptor or right before mass file writes is malicious. 2) Contain: isolate the host immediately and halt any active encryption; verify offline/immutable backups are intact. 3) Hunt: pivot to GentleKiller EDR-kill, wevtutil log clears and SystemBC C2 on the same host, and check other hosts for the same account.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where (FileName =~ "vssadmin.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "delete shadows")
   or (FileName =~ "wmic.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has_all ("shadowcopy","delete"))
   or (FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("Win32_Shadowcopy","Remove-WmiObject Win32_Shadowcopy"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where (NewProcessName endswith "vssadmin.exe" and CommandLine has "delete shadows")
   or (NewProcessName endswith "wmic.exe" and CommandLine has "shadowcopy" and CommandLine has "delete")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

SystemBC C2 beacon to The Gentlemen infrastructure IPs AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts outbound connections to SystemBC command-and-control IPs tied to The Gentlemen's bot-powered operation. SystemBC provides RC4-encrypted SOCKS5 tunneling; 45.86.230.112 is confirmed across Check Point and TheHackerNews reporting. Rationale: Article's C2 recommendation calls out SystemBC signatures; Check Point/TheHackerNews confirm SystemBC as The Gentlemen's proxy malware and confirm 45.86.230.112 as a C2, so the IOC set is second-source validated. Cross-checked against: • https://research.checkpoint.com/2026/dfir-report-the-gentlemen/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/04/systembc-c2-server-reveals-1570-victims.html • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/the-gentlemen-ransomware-now-uses-systembc-for-bot-powered-attacks/
ATT&CKT1090 T1571
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IP reassigned to a benign hosting tenant after the campaign (stale IOC)
  • Security researcher/sandbox deliberately connecting to the C2
  • Threat-intel scanner or honeypot beaconing to catalogue the host
  • Shared bulletproof-host IP later serving unrelated legitimate content
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process — SystemBC often runs as a renamed binary from Temp/ProgramData; confirm the destination is still attacker-controlled and not a stale/reassigned IP. 2) Contain: block the three IPs at the firewall, isolate the beaconing host, and capture the process binary and memory. 3) Hunt: sweep all hosts for connections to these IPs and to SystemBC's SOCKS5/RC4 pattern, then pivot to GentleKiller, wevtutil clears and shadow deletion to scope the intrusion.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP in ("45.86.230.112","193.233.202.17","77.110.122.137")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Protocol
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DestinationIP in ("45.86.230.112","193.233.202.17","77.110.122.137")
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, ApplicationProtocol, RequestURL, DeviceAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02

    selection_path:

            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'

    selection_file:

level: high

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.

Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;

| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)

| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",

          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"

   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("22b38dad7da097ea03aa28d0614164cd25fafeb1383dbc15047e34c8050f6f67", "51b9f246d6da85631131fcd1fabf0a67937d4bdde33625a44f7ee6a3a7baebd2", "025fc0976c548fb5a880c83ea3eb21a5f23c5d53c4e51e862bb893c11adf712a", "3ab9575225e00a83a4ac2b534da5a710bdcf6eb72884944c437b5fbe5c5c9235", "8ae6bd18b129061f63642531f1b684cf0383c75d", "d605994fc72a2bb59b5cfb1624a1b9170eca73a2", "5aa3124e5c4921e5edfc60133b5d71da21b07da3", "a5cf917ec4a7dfbdfa43621398604805d860c718") or SHA1 in~ ("22b38dad7da097ea03aa28d0614164cd25fafeb1383dbc15047e34c8050f6f67", "51b9f246d6da85631131fcd1fabf0a67937d4bdde33625a44f7ee6a3a7baebd2", "025fc0976c548fb5a880c83ea3eb21a5f23c5d53c4e51e862bb893c11adf712a", "3ab9575225e00a83a4ac2b534da5a710bdcf6eb72884944c437b5fbe5c5c9235", "8ae6bd18b129061f63642531f1b684cf0383c75d", "d605994fc72a2bb59b5cfb1624a1b9170eca73a2", "5aa3124e5c4921e5edfc60133b5d71da21b07da3", "a5cf917ec4a7dfbdfa43621398604805d860c718") or MD5 in~ ("22b38dad7da097ea03aa28d0614164cd25fafeb1383dbc15047e34c8050f6f67", "51b9f246d6da85631131fcd1fabf0a67937d4bdde33625a44f7ee6a3a7baebd2", "025fc0976c548fb5a880c83ea3eb21a5f23c5d53c4e51e862bb893c11adf712a", "3ab9575225e00a83a4ac2b534da5a710bdcf6eb72884944c437b5fbe5c5c9235", "8ae6bd18b129061f63642531f1b684cf0383c75d", "d605994fc72a2bb59b5cfb1624a1b9170eca73a2", "5aa3124e5c4921e5edfc60133b5d71da21b07da3", "a5cf917ec4a7dfbdfa43621398604805d860c718")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("22b38dad7da097ea03aa28d0614164cd25fafeb1383dbc15047e34c8050f6f67", "51b9f246d6da85631131fcd1fabf0a67937d4bdde33625a44f7ee6a3a7baebd2", "025fc0976c548fb5a880c83ea3eb21a5f23c5d53c4e51e862bb893c11adf712a", "3ab9575225e00a83a4ac2b534da5a710bdcf6eb72884944c437b5fbe5c5c9235", "8ae6bd18b129061f63642531f1b684cf0383c75d", "d605994fc72a2bb59b5cfb1624a1b9170eca73a2", "5aa3124e5c4921e5edfc60133b5d71da21b07da3", "a5cf917ec4a7dfbdfa43621398604805d860c718") or SHA1 in~ ("22b38dad7da097ea03aa28d0614164cd25fafeb1383dbc15047e34c8050f6f67", "51b9f246d6da85631131fcd1fabf0a67937d4bdde33625a44f7ee6a3a7baebd2", "025fc0976c548fb5a880c83ea3eb21a5f23c5d53c4e51e862bb893c11adf712a", "3ab9575225e00a83a4ac2b534da5a710bdcf6eb72884944c437b5fbe5c5c9235", "8ae6bd18b129061f63642531f1b684cf0383c75d", "d605994fc72a2bb59b5cfb1624a1b9170eca73a2", "5aa3124e5c4921e5edfc60133b5d71da21b07da3", "a5cf917ec4a7dfbdfa43621398604805d860c718") or MD5 in~ ("22b38dad7da097ea03aa28d0614164cd25fafeb1383dbc15047e34c8050f6f67", "51b9f246d6da85631131fcd1fabf0a67937d4bdde33625a44f7ee6a3a7baebd2", "025fc0976c548fb5a880c83ea3eb21a5f23c5d53c4e51e862bb893c11adf712a", "3ab9575225e00a83a4ac2b534da5a710bdcf6eb72884944c437b5fbe5c5c9235", "8ae6bd18b129061f63642531f1b684cf0383c75d", "d605994fc72a2bb59b5cfb1624a1b9170eca73a2", "5aa3124e5c4921e5edfc60133b5d71da21b07da3", "a5cf917ec4a7dfbdfa43621398604805d860c718")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["22b38dad7da097ea03aa28d0614164cd25fafeb1383dbc15047e34c8050f6f67", "51b9f246d6da85631131fcd1fabf0a67937d4bdde33625a44f7ee6a3a7baebd2", "025fc0976c548fb5a880c83ea3eb21a5f23c5d53c4e51e862bb893c11adf712a", "3ab9575225e00a83a4ac2b534da5a710bdcf6eb72884944c437b5fbe5c5c9235", "8ae6bd18b129061f63642531f1b684cf0383c75d", "d605994fc72a2bb59b5cfb1624a1b9170eca73a2", "5aa3124e5c4921e5edfc60133b5d71da21b07da3", "a5cf917ec4a7dfbdfa43621398604805d860c718"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → [LLM] Inventory of vulnerable TSDProxy deployments (pre-1.4.4 token-forwarding fix)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] TSDProxy management-API replay via injected x-tsdproxy-auth-token to loopback :8080 · [LLM] Unexpected process connecting to TSDProxy loopback management port 127.0.0.1:8080

TSDProxy management-API replay via injected x-tsdproxy-auth-token to loopback :8080 AIExploitation High
Hunts a backend-resident process replaying the leaked internal TSDProxy auth token to the localhost management API (127.0.0.1:8080/api/v1) with a spoofed x-tsdproxy-id, bypassing Tailscale auth to gain admin control. Article-specific because it keys on the exact forwarded header names and the loopback management endpoint. Rationale: Keys on the exact leaked-header names (x-tsdproxy-auth-token / x-tsdproxy-id) plus the loopback management endpoint (127.0.0.1:8080/api/v1) from the PoC — both are near-unique strings, so a match is almost certainly the token-replay attack. Cross-checked GitLab GLAD and cvereports for endpoint/port confirmation. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/almeidapaulopt/tsdproxy/GHSA-g936-7jqj-mwv8/ • https://cvereports.com/reports/GHSA-G936-7JQJ-MWV8
ATT&CKT1550.001 T1068
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • TSDProxy maintainer/QA running the documented PoC or a regression test that replays the token
  • Security team validating the patch by reproducing the exploit in a lab
  • Home-lab admin manually curling the management API with sample headers copied from the advisory
  • Automated integration test harness for tsdproxy that exercises /api/v1 with identity headers
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("tsdproxy") and AccountName !in~ ("tsdproxy")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process/container and confirm it is NOT the tsdproxy binary itself; pull the full ProcessCommandLine and the x-tsdproxy-id value used. 2) Contain: isolate the host/container, rotate the TSDProxy process auth token (restart tsdproxy) and set identityHeaders:false, then upgrade to >=1.4.4-0.20260603142855-434819b4421e. 3) Hunt: review /api/v1 access for proxy start/stop/pause and webhook-trigger calls (SSRF), enumerate which backends received the forwarded token, and check for prior /debug/headers-style token-capture requests on the same host.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("x-tsdproxy-auth-token","x-tsdproxy-id")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("127.0.0.1:8080","localhost:8080","/api/v1")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("x-tsdproxy-auth-token","x-tsdproxy-id")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("127.0.0.1:8080","localhost:8080","/api/v1")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: TSDProxy internal auth token replayed to loopback management API
id: 6b3e1f2a-9c74-4d0e-8f2a-1c5b7e9a2d41
description: Detects a process replaying the leaked x-tsdproxy-auth-token / spoofed x-tsdproxy-id header to the TSDProxy localhost management API (GHSA-g936-7jqj-mwv8)
references:
  - https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-g936-7jqj-mwv8
  - https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/almeidapaulopt/tsdproxy/GHSA-g936-7jqj-mwv8/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/12
tags:
  - attack.t1550.001
  - attack.t1068
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: linux
detection:
  sel_hdr:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - 'x-tsdproxy-auth-token'
      - 'x-tsdproxy-id'
  sel_target:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - '127.0.0.1:8080'
      - 'localhost:8080'
      - '/api/v1'
  condition: sel_hdr and sel_target
level: high
source:linux.auditd @auditd.type:EXECVE @process.command_line:(*x-tsdproxy-auth-token* OR *x-tsdproxy-id* OR *X-Tsdproxy-Auth-Token*) AND @process.command_line:(*127.0.0.1:8080* OR *localhost:8080* OR */api/v1*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| regex("(?i)x-tsdproxy-(auth-token|id)", field=CommandLine)
| regex("(127\\.0\\.0\\.1:8080|localhost:8080|/api/v1)", field=CommandLine)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process="*x-tsdproxy-auth-token*" OR Processes.process="*x-tsdproxy-id*") AND (Processes.process="*127.0.0.1:8080*" OR Processes.process="*localhost:8080*" OR Processes.process="*/api/v1*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process="*x-tsdproxy-auth-token*" OR Processes.process="*x-tsdproxy-id*") AND (Processes.process="*127.0.0.1:8080*" OR Processes.process="*localhost:8080*" OR Processes.process="*/api/v1*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Unexpected process connecting to TSDProxy loopback management port 127.0.0.1:8080 AIExploitation Medium
Network-shape variant that catches token replay performed with an HTTP library (python-requests, node, Go) where the header strings never hit a command line. Flags non-tsdproxy processes opening a loopback connection to the management port :8080, the interface the advisory says the management API binds to. Rationale: Catches the replay when the token is sent via an HTTP library (no header string in the cmdline) by pivoting on the loopback management port (:8080) named in the advisory, scoped to interpreter/CLI processes and excluding tsdproxy itself. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/almeidapaulopt/tsdproxy/GHSA-g936-7jqj-mwv8/
ATT&CKT1550.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate local health-check/monitoring script polling the tsdproxy management API on :8080
  • Another local web service (many apps default to :8080) being probed by curl during ops work
  • Container init/entrypoint scripts curling a co-located backend that also listens on 8080
  • Developer testing an API on localhost:8080 unrelated to tsdproxy
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("x-tsdproxy-auth-token","x-tsdproxy-id","/api/v1")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the destination :8080 process is the tsdproxy management server (not another app) and identify the connecting process and its container. 2) Contain: if the caller is an untrusted backend, isolate it, restart tsdproxy to rotate the token, and set identityHeaders:false. 3) Hunt: correlate the same source process with process-creation events for x-tsdproxy-auth-token strings (UC1) and review /api/v1 write operations that followed the connection.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where RemotePort == 8080
| where RemoteIP in ("127.0.0.1","::1")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("curl","wget","python","python3","ruby","node","perl","bash","sh","nc","ncat","socat")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("tsdproxy")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, LocalIP
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where DstPortNumber == 8080
| where DstIpAddr in ("127.0.0.1","::1")
| where SrcUsername != "tsdproxy"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcUsername, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkApplicationProtocol
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:linux.auditd @network.destination.port:8080 (@network.destination.ip:127.0.0.1 OR @network.destination.ip:::1) AND @process.name:(curl OR wget OR python OR python3 OR ruby OR node OR perl OR nc OR socat) -@process.name:tsdproxy
#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4 RemotePort=8080
| RemoteAddressIP4=/^127\.0\.0\.1$/
| regex("(?i)(curl|wget|python|ruby|node|perl|nc|ncat|socat)", field=ContextImageFileName)
| NOT ContextImageFileName=/tsdproxy/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, RemotePort], function=count())
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where All_Traffic.dest_port=8080 AND (All_Traffic.dest="127.0.0.1" OR All_Traffic.dest="::1") AND NOT All_Traffic.process_name="tsdproxy" by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.dest All_Traffic.dest_port All_Traffic.process_name All_Traffic.user | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where All_Traffic.dest_port=8080 AND (All_Traffic.dest="127.0.0.1" OR All_Traffic.dest="::1") AND NOT All_Traffic.process_name="tsdproxy" by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.dest All_Traffic.dest_port All_Traffic.process_name All_Traffic.user | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
TSDProxy forwarded-token harvesting via header-reflection endpoint or header grep AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the credential-access step where an attacker with backend code execution extracts the forwarded x-tsdproxy-auth-token — e.g. curling a header-reflection route (/debug/headers) and parsing the token out, or grepping/jq-ing it from request headers/logs. Article-specific because it keys on the exact header name and the PoC's reflection-endpoint capture technique. Rationale: Targets the PoC's token-capture step: fetching /debug/headers and parsing X-Tsdproxy-Auth-Token, or grepping/jq-ing the unique header name — distinct pivot from the replay (excludes 127.0.0.1:8080//api/v1 to avoid overlap with UC1). Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/almeidapaulopt/tsdproxy/GHSA-g936-7jqj-mwv8/
ATT&CKT1528
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer debugging identity headers by hitting a /debug/headers route legitimately
  • App observability tooling that logs or greps request headers for troubleshooting
  • Security tester reproducing the advisory's token-capture command in a lab
  • Log-analysis job that happens to grep header names across access logs
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full command line and the process/container; determine whether the token value was written to a file or piped onward. 2) Contain: treat the token as compromised — restart tsdproxy to rotate it, set identityHeaders:false, and upgrade to the fixed pseudo-version 1.4.4-0.20260603142855-434819b4421e. 3) Hunt: pivot to the same host for a subsequent replay to 127.0.0.1:8080/api/v1 (UC1/UC2) and review webhook/proxy config enumeration that would follow successful admin access.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "/debug/headers"
    or (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("x-tsdproxy-auth-token","X-Tsdproxy-Auth-Token")
        and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("grep","awk","jq","python","python3","cut","tcpdump","json.load"))
| where not(ProcessCommandLine has_any ("127.0.0.1:8080","/api/v1"))  // exclude the replay step (UC1)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "/debug/headers"
    or (ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("x-tsdproxy-auth-token","X-Tsdproxy-Auth-Token")
        and ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("grep","awk","jq","python","python3","cut","tcpdump"))
| where not(ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("127.0.0.1:8080","/api/v1"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Inventory of vulnerable TSDProxy deployments (pre-1.4.4 token-forwarding fix) AIReconnaissance Medium
Surfaces hosts/containers running TSDProxy so the SOC can confirm the version is below the fixed Go pseudo-version 1.4.4-0.20260603142855-434819b4421e and that identityHeaders is not set to false. Supports the article's mitigation guidance (upgrade + disable identity-header forwarding). Rationale: Uses the exact affected package (github.com/almeidapaulopt/tsdproxy) and the specific fixed pseudo-version from the advisory to build a targeted exposure inventory; process-presence fallback covers hosts where TVM does not catalogue the Go binary. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/almeidapaulopt/tsdproxy/GHSA-g936-7jqj-mwv8/ • https://github.com/almeidapaulopt/tsdproxy

Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Host already upgraded to >=1.4.4-0.20260603142855-434819b4421e (not actually vulnerable)
  • Deployment that has already set identityHeaders:false (mitigated despite old version)
  • A binary named tsdproxy that is a fork or unrelated wrapper
  • TVM version string formatted differently from the Go pseudo-version, complicating comparison
Response runbook
1) Triage: for each hit, capture SoftwareVersion (or query the running binary --version) and read the proxy config for identityHeaders. 2) Contain: on vulnerable+default hosts, set identityHeaders:false immediately and schedule upgrade to the fixed pseudo-version. 3) Hunt: on any confirmed-vulnerable host, retro-hunt UC1/UC3 for token replay/harvesting since the deployment date and audit which backends were proxied.
DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory
| where SoftwareName has "tsdproxy" or SoftwareVendor has "almeidapaulopt"
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, Timestamp
| order by Timestamp desc
// Vulnerable if SoftwareVersion precedes 1.4.4-0.20260603142855-434819b4421e; verify identityHeaders is set to false in the proxy config
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where SoftwareName has "tsdproxy" or SoftwareVendor has "almeidapaulopt"
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, OSPlatform, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:linux.auditd @auditd.type:EXECVE (@process.name:tsdproxy OR @process.executable.path:*tsdproxy*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/tsdproxy$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name="tsdproxy" OR Processes.process="*tsdproxy*" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name="tsdproxy" OR Processes.process="*tsdproxy*" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)

Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] SiYuan Electron renderer spawns shell/LOLBin (stored-XSS-to-RCE via nodeIntegration)

Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
SiYuan Electron renderer spawns shell/LOLBin (stored-XSS-to-RCE via nodeIntegration) AIExploitation High
Hunts the RCE stage of CVE-2026-50551/CVE-2026-54158: a stored XSS payload in an attribute-view cell fires in SiYuan's Electron renderer, which runs with nodeIntegration:true and reaches require('child_process') to spawn arbitrary host commands. SiYuan is a note-taking app and should never parent cmd/powershell/wscript, so any such child is high-fidelity RCE. Rationale: Uses the exact article-named parent binary (SiYuan.exe) and the nodeIntegration→child_process RCE chain; a knowledge-management Electron app spawning interpreters is near-zero baseline, making the parent→child pair high-fidelity. Cross-checked GitLab Advisory DB (CVE-2026-54158) and the SiYuan GitHub security advisories confirming the same nodeIntegration:true/contextIsolation:false config across the CVE family. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/siyuan-note/siyuan/kernel/CVE-2026-54158/ • https://github.com/siyuan-note/siyuan/security/advisories/GHSA-phhp-9rm9-6gr2 • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/siyuan-note/siyuan/kernel/CVE-2026-50551/
ATT&CKT1203 T1059.007 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • SiYuan community plugins that legitimately shell out (e.g. export-to-PDF, git-sync, or pandoc integration plugins invoking node/cmd)
  • Developers running SiYuan from source spawning node.exe during build/watch
  • SiYuan auto-updater launching a helper/installer process on version upgrade
  • Security tooling injecting into or wrapping SiYuan.exe and inheriting the parent name
  • conhost.exe host allocation appearing as a benign child on interpreter launch
Suppression filter
| where not (FileName =~ "conhost.exe") | where not (FileName =~ "node.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("--build","electron","webpack"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full child ProcessCommandLine and grandchild tree on the host; benign plugin activity has recognisable args (pandoc, git, node build), whereas RCE shows encoded PowerShell, downloaders, or discovery commands. Confirm SiYuan version < 3.7.0 (vulnerable). 2) Contain: isolate the endpoint, kill the SiYuan process tree, and quarantine the user's workspace `data/storage/av/*.json` files before they re-sync to other devices. 3) Hunt: enumerate every device sharing that user's SiYuan sync/workspace (this bug fires on every peer that opens the poisoned row), review those hosts for the same SiYuan.exe child-process pattern and any outbound C2 from the spawned child.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "SiYuan.exe"
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe","curl.exe","node.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith @"\SiYuan.exe"
| where NewProcessName has_any (@"\cmd.exe",@"\powershell.exe",@"\pwsh.exe",@"\wscript.exe",@"\cscript.exe",@"\mshta.exe",@"\rundll32.exe",@"\regsvr32.exe",@"\certutil.exe",@"\bitsadmin.exe",@"\curl.exe",@"\node.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

  condition: selection
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @ParentImage:(*\SiYuan.exe OR *\siyuan.exe OR *\SIYUAN.EXE) @Image:(*\cmd.exe OR *\powershell.exe OR *\PowerShell.exe OR *\pwsh.exe OR *\wscript.exe OR *\cscript.exe OR *\mshta.exe OR *\rundll32.exe OR *\regsvr32.exe OR *\certutil.exe OR *\bitsadmin.exe OR *\curl.exe OR *\node.exe)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ParentBaseFileName=/siyuan\.exe$/i
| ImageFileName=/\\(cmd|powershell|pwsh|wscript|cscript|mshta|rundll32|regsvr32|certutil|bitsadmin|curl|node)\.exe$/i

Out-of-band write to SiYuan attribute-view store (data/storage/av/*.json payload plant) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the persistence/plant stage of CVE-2026-50551: the malicious attribute-view cell is written to data/storage/av/<avID>.json and rides workspace sync to every peer. A process other than SiYuan.exe writing to that exact store path indicates manual/malware staging of the payload or an external sync client propagating a poisoned AV file. Rationale: Anchors on the article's exact backing-store path data/storage/av/<avID>.json plus the fact that only SiYuan.exe should author those files; a foreign writer surfaces manual PoC-style plants and malware staging the poisoned AV JSON. Corroborated against the SiYuan GitHub advisory and GitLab Advisory DB confirming the storage path and sync-propagation model. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/siyuan-note/siyuan/kernel/CVE-2026-54158/ • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/siyuan-note/siyuan/kernel/CVE-2026-50551/
ATT&CKT1565.001 T1608.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Third-party sync clients (Dropbox.exe, OneDrive.exe, Syncthing.exe, Resilio) writing the workspace JSON — note these are ALSO the legitimate payload-propagation vector, so triage rather than blanket-exclude
  • Backup/restore software (Veeam, Duplicati, robocopy) copying the workspace into place
  • User manually restoring a workspace snapshot or migrating between machines
  • Antivirus/EDR remediation rewriting the file after a scan
  • Text editors or scripts a power-user runs to bulk-edit their own SiYuan database
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("OneDrive.exe","Dropbox.exe","Syncthing.exe","ResilioSync.exe","robocopy.exe","MsMpEng.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: retrieve the written data/storage/av/*.json and grep the cell content for HTML breakout patterns (</textarea>, "><img, src=x, onerror=, <script); a benign SiYuan AV file contains none. Identify the writing process — if it is a sync client, treat as propagation and pivot to origin. 2) Contain: quarantine the offending JSON, block the SiYuan sync channel for the affected workspace, and prevent peers from opening the block-attribute panel until cleaned. 3) Hunt: on every device sharing that workspace, look for the paired RCE signal (UC: SiYuan.exe spawning cmd/powershell/node) and confirm all endpoints are upgraded to SiYuan >= 3.7.0.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FolderPath has @"\data\storage\av\"
| where FileName endswith ".json"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("SiYuan.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where TargetFilePath has @"\data\storage\av\"
| where TargetFileName endswith ".json"
| where ActingProcessName !has "SiYuan.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, DvcAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
